hero.title: Chemical Reactions & Equations — Chemistry in Action
hero.hook: Iron rusting, wood burning, food cooking, bleaching clothes, medicine working in your body — all of these are chemical reactions. Chapter 1 of Class 10 Science isn't just about balancing equations. It's about understanding what types of changes are happening and why. Every board exam starts here.

hook_section.scenario: Drop a piece of magnesium ribbon in hydrochloric acid. Within seconds: vigorous bubbling, the magnesium dissolves, the solution warms up. What happened? A new substance formed (MgCl₂), a gas was released (H₂), energy was released (heat). These observations — new substance, energy change, gas, precipitate — are signs that a chemical reaction occurred.
hook_section.bridge: Chapter 1 covers how to write and balance chemical equations, types of reactions (combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, oxidation-reduction), and indicators of chemical change. The 5-6 mark equations question at the end of a paper almost always starts with one of these reaction types.
hook_section.punchline: Balance atoms, not charges — same number of each element on both sides. Types of reactions have tell-tale patterns: learn to identify them from the equation structure.

concept_section.analogy: Chemical reactions are like theatrical performances. Combination is a marriage (two become one). Decomposition is a divorce (one splits into two). Displacement is an eviction (a stronger element pushes a weaker one out of a compound). Double displacement is a partner swap (two compounds exchange partners). Oxidation-reduction always happen together — one gains oxygen/loses hydrogen while the other does the opposite.
concept_section.principle: Law of Conservation of Mass: matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Balanced equations have same atoms of each element on both sides. Symbols of state: (s)=solid, (l)=liquid, (g)=gas, (aq)=aqueous solution.
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each reaction type to identify and memorise 👇

reveals.question: 🤝 Combination & Decomposition?
reveals.answer: Combination (Synthesis): A + B → AB. CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (exothermic). C + O₂ → CO₂. Decomposition: AB → A + B. 2FeSO₄ → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂ + SO₃ (thermal). 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (photochemical — used in photography). 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electrolytic).

reveals.question: 🔄 Displacement & Double Displacement?
reveals.answer: Single Displacement: A + BC → AC + B. Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (iron displaces copper — reactivity series). Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Double Displacement (usually precipitate or gas forms): Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O (neutralisation).

reveals.question: 🔥 Oxidation & Reduction (Redox)?
reveals.answer: Oxidation: gain of oxygen / loss of hydrogen / loss of electrons. Reduction: loss of oxygen / gain of hydrogen / gain of electrons. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Redox: both happen simultaneously. Example: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (CuO reduced, H₂ oxidised).

reveals.question: 🌿 Exothermic vs Endothermic?
reveals.answer: Exothermic: energy released as heat (temperature rises). Examples: combustion, neutralisation, respiration, quick lime + water. Endothermic: energy absorbed (temperature drops). Examples: decomposition, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium chloride in water, baking soda + acid.

points: Balanced equation: atoms conserved on both sides; mass is neither created nor destroyed
Double displacement: exchange of ions, often forms precipitate (↓) or gas (↑)
Redox: oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously; OIL RIG mnemonic

exam_questions.question: Balance the equation: Fe₂O₃ + Al → Al₂O₃ + Fe. Identify the type of reaction and which substance is oxidised and which is reduced.
What is a redox reaction? Give one example with the equation.
What type of chemical reaction takes place when quicklime is added to water?

quiz.q: 2FeSO₄ → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂ + SO₃ is an example of:
quiz.exp: One compound (FeSO₄) breaks down into three products. This is a thermal decomposition reaction — breaking apart by heating. The ↑ symbol would indicate gases evolved.

quiz.q: In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, which is oxidised?
quiz.exp: H₂ gains oxygen (H₂ → H₂O) — this is oxidation (OIL = Oxidation Is Loss, here gaining O, which is oxidation). CuO loses oxygen (CuO → Cu) — this is reduction. CuO is the oxidising agent; H₂ is the reducing agent.

quiz.q: AgCl decomposes in sunlight to form Ag and Cl₂. This is:
quiz.exp: Photochemical decomposition is triggered by light (photo = light). AgCl and AgBr decompose in sunlight to form silver. This principle is used in black-and-white photography.

quiz.q: What does the symbol (aq) represent in a chemical equation?
quiz.exp: (aq) = aqueous solution. The states of matter in equations are: (s)=solid, (l)=liquid, (g)=gas, (aq)=dissolved in water. These state symbols provide crucial extra information.

flipcards.front: What is the law of conservation of mass?
flipcards.back: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — total mass of reactants = total mass of products
Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons) | Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)
Single displacement reaction — zinc displaces copper (zinc is more reactive than copper in the activity series)
Exothermic: energy released (combustion, neutralisation). Endothermic: energy absorbed (decomposition, photosynthesis)
An insoluble solid formed during a double displacement reaction (shown by ↓ symbol)
2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (in sunlight). Used in photography — silver deposited where light strikes.
